# Adjacent-Domain Practice and Requirement Nuggets

Dimension 4: what machinery-safety standards, industrial collision sensors
and observatory interlocks say that maps onto a latching collision kill
switch. Includes counter-perspectives. Sources: [citations](../citations.md).

## Scope caveat

ISO 13850 defines an emergency stop as a function "initiated by a single
human action" [68]. A switch tripped by contact is therefore not an E-stop
in the strict sense. It is closer to the pressure-sensitive trip devices of
ISO 13856 [78]. The requirements below are borrowed by analogy. Neither
standard applies directly to amateur equipment protection.

## Candidate requirements

IDs use an `E` prefix to keep them distinct from the R-numbered list in the
[main analysis](../strain-wave-mount-collision-kill-switch.md).

| # | Candidate requirement | Basis (quote) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | Trip latches until manually reset | "it shall be maintained until it is manually reset" | [68] §4.1.1.2 |
| E2 | No start command works while tripped | "it shall not be possible for any start command to be effective" | [68] §4.1.1.2 |
| E3 | Reset must not restart motion | "The reset shall not initiate machine start up." | [68] §4.1.1.2; [71]; [72] |
| E4 | Reset at the device that tripped, by deliberate action, after the hazard is cleared | "may only be reset directly on the emergency stop device on which the command was initiated and by intentional human action" | [70] |
| E5 | The stop must not create a new hazard | stop "without creating additional hazards" | [68] §4.1.1.5 |
| E6 | The stop must not disable other safety functions such as brakes | "it can be necessary to ensure the continuing operation of auxiliary equipment such as... braking devices" | [68] §4.1.1.4 |
| E7 | It is a complement to limits, not a substitute | "complementary protective measure" | [68] §4.1.1.3 |
| E8 | Fail-safe NC wiring: a broken wire or contact trips | NC "provides an additional safety in case of failure" | [80]; [5] |
| E9 | Positive-opening contacts: separation forced mechanically, not by a spring; actuator breaks a weld | "must not depend on components such as springs"; "the action of the actuator will mechanically break the weld" | [76], [77] |
| E10 | Cut power downstream of every controller | "Any critical failsafe control is always properly done outside of and downstream (power wise) of the controller" | [8] |
| E11 | Release, reset and restart are three separate steps | "The mere fact that the cycle does not restart automatically is not sufficient." | [73] |
| E12 | Reliability target for real E-stops: PL c; single channel can suffice | "single-channel architectures can achieve the required Performance Level with suitable component selection" | [71] |

## Stop category mapping

- Category 0 is "stopping by immediate cutting off of power to the
  actuators (example: uncontrolled stop)" [74].
- GT Engineering: "Machines with moving parts without inertia and whose
  stop does not cause additional risks require stop in Category 0"; a
  Category 0 E-stop "is equivalent to the STO (Safe Torque Off) function"
  [75].
- STO "does not mechanically lock the axis" [59].
- [75] also says that for machines with inertia, or that need other safety
  systems, "stop in Category 1 is required".
- **Mapping (inference).** The proposed switch is a Category 0 stop. A
  slewing mount has inertia (see the flywheel remark in [21]), and an
  unbraked DEC can back-drive once unpowered (see
  [power-loss-behavior.md](power-loss-behavior.md)). By [75]'s criteria,
  that points toward Category 1. A controlled (Category 1) stop needs the
  mount's own firmware, which an external switch cannot provide. The
  standards were written for personnel safety, so this is guidance by
  analogy, not a binding rule for amateur equipment.

## Contact-device geometry (ISO 13856-2 terms)

ISO 13856-2 defines "pre-travel" (travel from contact to output OFF) and
"overtravel" [78]. **Inference:** the mount's coast after the cut, which
the [21] flywheel comment suggests is non-zero, has to fit within the
switch's overtravel. Otherwise contact force keeps rising after the trip.
No source measures mount coast distance.

## Industrial collision-sensor practice

| Product | Output | Reset | Speed claim | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RAD Ultimatic | Opens an NC switch to E-stop or controller | Automatic | "within 2 to 10ms" (footnote not captured) | [81] |
| ATI Protector | Signal to robot controller | Automatic | Not captured | [82] |
| SCHUNK OPS | Signal "without delay" | Not stated | Not stated | [83] |
| Harmonic Drive torque-sensor gear | Torque signal for "collision detection" | Controller-defined | 0.1% FS accuracy (vendor) | [65] |
| Agility slip-clutch patent | Mechanical slip above a torque threshold | Mechanical | — | [67] |

Industry pairs the contact sensor with a controller and resets
automatically. The proposal deliberately departs from this with a latched,
manual reset and no controller.

## Counter-perspectives

1. **Contact means the collision has already started.** "the collision
   already happened" [11]. Gear damage from overload can occur "in a
   millisecond" [63], and a ratcheted drive "is permanently altered" [63].
2. **Stopped input under load.** With the input shaft stationary and an
   excessive load applied, "the FS tends to experience buckling" [64]. A
   powered-off mount that is still pressed against an obstacle is in this
   state (inference).
3. **Brakes are not stopping devices.** Holding brakes used to stop a
   moving shaft cause "potentially damaging" backlash [58].
4. **Power cut breaks software.** Dropping mount power upsets everything
   connected to it [9].
5. **False trips.** Sensors can give false readings [11]. The builder of an
   accelerometer power-cut device notes that legitimate ASIAIR flips come
   within about 5 mm of the tripod, so the device "has to pretty accurate" to
   avoid unnecessary stops [1]. The build was shelved, partly over the
   difficulty of training the no-go zone [1].
6. **Current sensing might be enough.** Several posters favour a current
   cutoff [2]. Others doubt that the current change is detectable through
   high gear ratios [2]. ZWO's stall detection is off at tracking speed [22].

## Gaps and Limitations

- The ISO 13850 and ISO 13856-2 texts are previews that stop at §4.1.1.6
  and §4.1. ISO 13850:2015 is marked "To be revised" [69]. ISO 13856-2:2013
  was confirmed in 2024 [79]. Clauses on stop categories, latching device design and reset
  timing were not read.
- IEC 60204-1, IEC 60947-5-1 and IEC 60947-5-5 were read only through vendor
  explainers [72], [74], [75], [76], [77].
- The "only stop categories 0 and 1 for E-stop" claim rests on one vendor
  source [75] and is not used as a requirement here.
- No source gives contact-to-cutoff timing for any astro setup, or
  momentary peak torque ratings for mount gears.
